name: Haizumi

lead: Haizumi is a soot-based powder ink used by aristocratic Japanese women, especially in the Heian period, to draw eyebrows high on the forehead after plucking or shaving the natural ones. It is the pigment behind the hikimayu look.
The soot came from burning sesame or rapeseed oil. The painted brows were part of a courtly style that also included white face powder and blackened teeth.

paras: In the historical practice the natural brows were removed first, then oval or smudge-shaped brows were painted on the upper forehead with haizumi. Today the look appears mostly in Noh and kabuki, historical performance and festivals.
The practice was part of a total makeup style with white powder and ohaguro tooth dye. Japan banned hikimayu and ohaguro in 1870. No health research on haizumi itself is described in the sources.

angle.text: Haizumi gave the painted brows that completed the Heian court face: white powder, dark teeth and brows set high on the forehead. It remains a reference for historical and theatrical makeup.

lead: Haizumi is a powdered ink made from soot produced by burning sesame or rapeseed oil. Aristocratic Japanese women used it to draw new eyebrows after removing their natural ones, a practice called hikimayu.[1]

Hikimayu began in the 8th century when the Japanese court adopted Chinese customs, with early brows painted as arcs. Heian-period women later painted ovals or smudges high on the forehead.[1] One theory says this balanced the prominent forehead created by long hair worn loose at the sides, though it is unconfirmed.[1] Another proposal is that removing natural brows made applying white face powder easier.[1]

Later in the Heian period men at court also whitened faces, blackened teeth and redrew brows.[1] The look appears in Noh masks of young female roles and in classics such as The Tale of Genji, and was banned by the government in 1870.[1][2]
infobox: Burnt sesame or rapeseed oil soot[1]

paras: Haizumi is the black powdered ink used to paint eyebrows in hikimayu, which means pulling out the brows.[1] It was made from the soot of burning sesame or rapeseed oil.[1]

The practice appeared in the 8th century and became most fashionable in the Heian period (794-1185).[1] In the Edo period (1603-1867) it became associated with married women.[1] After Japan opened to Western culture the government banned hikimayu and ohaguro in 1870.[1][2]
Painted brows were worn with oshiroi white powder and ohaguro tooth blackening. Some scholars link the masklike combination to a cultural preference for concealing emotion.[2]

Today hikimayu appears in Noh and kabuki, historical performance and occasional local festivals, and apprentice geisha in Kyoto may still practise ohaguro.[1] It features in the films Rashomon, Ugetsu and Ran.[1]
